```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5
)
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(unimlsurv)
  library(mlr3)
})
```

`unimlsurv` is the time-to-event counterpart to `uniml`. It keeps the same
layering — specification, data, task, learners, tuning, metrics, plots,
workflow — so if you know one package you know the other. What changes is the
outcome and therefore what "correct" means.

This vignette uses a simulated cohort with a known truth throughout, so every
number can be checked against the model that generated it. A companion
vignette, `vignette("unimlsurv-metrics", package = "unimlsurv")`, walks through
each metric one at a time with more explanation and fewer moving parts.

## What a survival outcome is

Two columns, not one:

* the follow-up **time**: how long a patient was observed;
* the **status**: `1` if the event happened at that time, `0` if the patient was
  censored at that time.

Censoring is why survival statistics are not classification statistics. A
patient censored at 10 months is not a patient who survived 10 months and it is
not a patient who died at 10 months — the observation says "no event *yet*",
which is why every metric in this package either drops censored patients from a
comparison they cannot inform (the concordance index) or weights them by the
inverse of the censoring survival (Brier score, time-dependent AUC,
calibration, decision curves). Ignoring censoring is the most common way a
survival paper gets its numbers wrong.

```{r data}
data <- sim_surv_data(n = 400, seed = 2026)
head(data, 4)
table(data$status)
```

The simulator stores the true linear predictor, so we can also ask what the
best possible answer looks like:

```{r truth}
time_points <- c(3, 6, 12)
truth <- sim_surv_truth(data, time_points)
round(head(truth$survival, 3), 3)
```

**The time points are yours to choose.** They should be the horizons a
clinician would ask about, and they must be horizons the follow-up can
support: a time point past which nobody was observed has no comparable pairs
left, and the package reports `NA` there rather than inventing a number. With
this cohort's median follow-up around 4 months, horizons of 3, 6 and 12 are
supported; horizons of 36 or 60 would not be.

## The specification comes first

`surv_spec()` builds a `uniml_spec` with `task_type = "survival"` and adds a
`survival` block. Preprocessing, tuning, and learners are configured with the
same functions as in `uniml`, because they are the same functions.

```{r spec}
spec <- surv_spec(
  time = "time",
  status = "status",
  time_points = time_points
)
spec <- uniml::set_preprocess(spec, impute = "median_mode", scale = "zscore")
spec <- surv_set_learners(spec, c("coxph", "kaplan"), tune = FALSE)
spec
```

`kaplan` is here on purpose: it is the covariate-free baseline, the model
that must score exactly 0.5 on the concordance index — the built-in sanity
check every survival comparison deserves. `surv_learner_registry()` lists
every native engine; advanced users can register mlr3 learners with
`surv_register_learner()`.

## Data and task

```{r task}
prepared <- as_surv_data(data, spec)
prepared

task <- make_surv_task(prepared, spec)
task
```

`as_surv_data()` drops rows with a missing time or status rather than imputing
them: an imputed outcome is not an outcome. Feature values may still be missing,
and those are imputed during preprocessing, on the training data only.

## The metrics, one at a time

```{r metrics}
fitted <- train_surv(task, resolve_surv_learners("coxph", tune = FALSE)$coxph$learner)
prediction <- predict_surv_learner(fitted, prepared$data, time_points)

survival <- survival_matrix(prediction, time_points)
risk <- survival_risk(prediction)

metrics <- calc_surv_metrics(
  prepared$time, prepared$status, risk, survival, time_points
)
metrics$overall
metrics$by_time
```

Read the table like this:

* `cindex` is Harrell's concordance index: pick two patients where one had the
  event first; the C-index is the probability the model gave the sicker one the
  higher risk. 0.5 is a coin flip. Its weakness is that the set of comparable
  pairs depends on *who got censored*, so two cohorts with the same model can
  give different C-indices for censoring reasons alone.
* `uno_c` is the censoring-adjusted answer to the same question (Uno et al.
  2011). It reweights the pairs by the inverse **squared** censoring survival
  estimated on the **training** data and truncates at `tau`. Report Harrell's C
  and Uno's C side by side; when they disagree, the disagreement is about the
  censoring, not about the model. Both need only a risk score, which is why the
engines that only output a risk score (a registered foreign learner) would get them and nothing else.
* `brier(t)` is the inverse-probability-of-censoring weighted mean squared
  difference between the predicted survival probability and what happened.
  Lower is better.
* `ibs` integrates the Brier score over the time points you asked for with the
  trapezoidal rule — it therefore depends on that grid, and the documentation
  says so.
* `auc(t)` is the cumulative/dynamic AUC: the probability that a patient who
  had an event by `t` was given a higher risk than a patient who was still
  event-free after it.
* `auc_uno(t)` is Uno's IPCW estimator of the same quantity: same pairs, but
  the case weights come from the **training** censoring curve. When the
  evaluation set is small, `auc` and `auc_uno` can disagree for censoring
  reasons; report both and say which one a table uses.
* `iauc` and `iauc_uno` integrate the two AUC families over your grid.
* The calibration columns (`citl`, `e50`, `e90`) are explained in the next
  section.

Every one of these is pinned by a test against an independent implementation:
`survival::concordance()` for Harrell's C, `survAUC::UnoC()` and
`survAUC::AUC.uno()` for the Uno statistics (agreement to machine precision),
`riskRegression::Score()` for the Brier score and the AUC. The AUC is
additionally pinned against the area under the ROC curve the package itself
draws, so the number and the figure cannot disagree.

## Calibration: is the number right?

Discrimination asks "who is sicker"; calibration asks "is the number right". A
model can rank perfectly and still tell every patient they have a 90% chance of
surviving.

```{r calibration}
calibration <- surv_calibration_curves(
  prepared$time, prepared$status, survival, time_points
)
calibration$summary
```

* `ici` is the integrated calibration index: the patient-weighted mean absolute
  difference between the prediction and the Kaplan-Meier estimate inside each
  prediction group.
* `citl` is calibration-in-the-large: the group-size-weighted mean of
  `observed - predicted`. Negative means the predictions run too high on
  average. It is the closest thing to the binary intercept.
* `e50` and `e90` are the median and the 90th percentile of the patient-level
  absolute error, where each patient's observed value is the Kaplan-Meier
  estimate of their prediction group. The trio is from Austin and colleagues
  (2019, 2020): a large ICI with a small E50 means a few groups are badly off;
  the reverse means small errors are spread everywhere.
* The summary also carries `slope` and `intercept`, which answer a sharper
  question than the group table and do not depend on how the groups were cut:

```{r calibration-slope}
surv_calibration_slope(prepared$time, prepared$status, survival[, 1],
                       time_points[1])
```

`surv_calibration_slope()` fits
`cloglog(P(T <= t | x)) = intercept + slope * cloglog(1 - S(t | x))`. A
calibrated prediction gives a slope of 1 and an intercept of 0. Below 1 means
the predictions are too extreme, above 1 means too timid. **Read `n` and
`events` before the coefficients**: this cohort has enough patients, but a
slope from a few dozen patients can sit far from 1 while the model is fine.
Roughly 100 patients with a few dozen events is where the number starts to mean
something.

```{r calibration-plot, fig.cap = "Time-point calibration against Kaplan-Meier survival, with the recalibration coefficients in the caption."}
plot_surv_calibration(calibration)
```

## Discrimination over time and risk strata

```{r km, fig.cap = "Kaplan-Meier curves by simulated risk tercile, with the log-rank p-value."}
frame <- prepared
frame$risk_group <- surv_risk_groups(risk, k = 3)
plot_surv_km(frame, spec, group = "risk_group", logrank = TRUE)
```

The stratified Kaplan-Meier figure is what prediction papers show: split the
cohort by predicted risk into equal-sized groups and draw one curve per group,
with a log-rank p-value. The groups are a *presentation* device — their
boundaries depend on the sample and must never be reused as clinical
thresholds. The underlying model comparison lives in the metrics tables.

## Decision curves

A model is only useful if acting on it beats acting on everybody and beats
acting on nobody.

```{r dca}
dca <- surv_dca_curves(prepared$time, prepared$status, survival, time_points)
plot_surv_dca(dca)
```

Net benefit is computed with the same inverse-probability-of-censoring weights,
so a patient censored before the horizon is not counted as a certain non-event.

## The workflow

`run_surv_workflow()` runs the shared `uniml` engine — the same code that
prepares, tunes, and predicts for the binary workflow — and then scores the
results with the survival metrics. The validation set selects, the test and
external sets report.

```{r workflow}
set.seed(42)
index <- sample.int(nrow(data))
train <- data[index[1:280], ]
validation <- data[index[281:340], ]
test <- data[index[341:400], ]

result <- run_surv_workflow(spec, train = train, validation = validation,
                            test = test, ci_R = 100)

result$metrics[, c("model", "set", "cindex", "uno_c", "ibs", "iauc",
                   "iauc_uno")]
result$ranking
```

A registered foreign learner that outputs only a risk score reports a C-index
and Uno's C and nothing else. That is not a bug: such a learner cannot be
asked for a Brier score. The package says so in `result$meta$notes` instead
of quietly filling in a number.

```{r notes}
result$meta$notes
```

Every per-time column — `brier_3`, `auc_3`, `auc_uno_3`, `citl_3`, `e50_3`,
`e90_3`, and the recalibration coefficients — lives in `result$metrics` as
well, and `result$meta$by_time` holds the long table. `surv_ci()` bootstraps
every column automatically:

```{r ci}
head(result$ci[, c("model", "metric", "mean", "lower", "upper",
                   "n_effective")], 8)
```

Patients are resampled, not rows of a metric table. A resample that loses the
cases or the controls a time point needs returns `NA` and is counted in
`n_effective`, so a narrow interval can never come from a handful of lucky
resamples.

## Explaining the model

A survival model does not predict one number, so a SHAP analysis has to say
what it is explaining. `time_point = NULL` explains the risk score — the
quantity the concordance index ranks. A time point explains the predicted
survival probability at that horizon instead. Since version 0.3.0 the
explanations are reported **per variable**, not per one-hot column: the
`sex_female`/`sex_male` columns of the encoder are summed back to `sex`, the
same convention published SHAP figures use.

```{r shap-risk}
explained <- surv_shap(
  result, newdata = validation, model = "coxph",
  n_explain = 40, bg_n = 20, seed = 1
)
plot_surv_shap_importance(explained)
```

```{r shap-time, fig.cap = "SHAP dependence for the predicted 6-month survival."}
explained_6 <- surv_shap(
  result, newdata = validation, model = "coxph", time_point = 6,
  n_explain = 40, bg_n = 20, seed = 1
)
plot_surv_shap_dependence(explained_6, "x1")
```

The two explanations are not interchangeable: a feature can raise the risk
score and lower S(6) by different relative amounts, and the ranking of features
can differ between them. Report which quantity you explained.

## Handing the model to someone else

Subgroup analyses are not part of this package on purpose: which subgroups
matter is a clinical decision, and a package that guesses is worse than one
that does not. What the package does is hand over everything needed to do it
properly.

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
path <- uniml::save_result(result, "model.rds")
```

The file holds the fitted learners, the fitted preprocessor, the selected
features, and the specification. Whoever opens it can score any subset and use
the same metric functions the workflow used:

```{r subgroup, eval = FALSE}
restored <- uniml::read_result("model.rds")
older <- validation[validation$age > 50, ]
scored <- predict_surv(restored, older)
calc_surv_metrics(
  older$time, older$status, scored$risk,
  as.matrix(scored[, grep("^S_", names(scored))]),
  restored$meta$time_points
)
```

Predicting new patients uses the fitted preprocessor and the fitted learner,
and never refits anything on the new data:

```{r predict}
newdata <- data[index[341:350], ]
predict_surv(result, newdata, model = "coxph")
```

A registered risk-only learner would be rejected here: the error names the
which cannot produce survival probabilities. The error names the models that
can, which is more useful than silently switching to a different model than
you asked for.

## Exporting a result

The result is a `uniml_result`, so the export layout is the one you already
know:

```{r export, eval = FALSE}
uniml::export_results(result, dir = "report")
```

## Which learners are available

`surv_learner_registry()` lists every `surv.*` learner the installed `mlr3`
packages expose, with a short alias, whether it can produce survival
probabilities, and whether it has a curated tuning search space.

```{r registry}
available <- surv_learner_registry(available_only = TRUE)
available[, c("key", "engine", "distr", "tunable")]
```

The native registry ships coxph and kaplan; surv_register_learner() adds
whatever else you want — another native engine with different defaults, or a
foreign mlr3 survival learner (the advanced path that needs the GitHub-only
mlr3proba package).

## What is deliberately missing

* **Competing risks.** A patient who dies of something else is not censored;
  they had an event, of a different type. That changes the estimate, not just
  the implementation, so it is out of scope here.
* **Net reclassification improvement.** NRI compares two models on the same
  data; the Steyerberg framework reserves it for the "does a new marker add
  value on top of an established model" question, not for reporting one model.
* **D-calibration and IPCW log-loss.** Rarely reported in prediction papers;
  both can be computed directly if a reviewer asks.
* **Distribution composition.** A risk-only learner can be handed a full
  survival distribution by borrowing a baseline from another learner — a
  trick mlr3proba's PipeOpDistrCompositor automates. That changes what "the
  model's Brier score" means, so it is a separate, opt-in design decision
  rather than a default here.
* **Tuning on the Brier score.** The inverse-probability weights depend on the
  censoring distribution of the data the model was fitted on, so tuning models
  on it would compare numbers computed on different data. Tuning uses the
  concordance index.

See `system.file("REFERENCES.md", package = "unimlsurv")` for the full list of
papers each statistic follows, with verified DOIs.
